# Four types {background-color="#0C234B"}

## The ones that matter

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
#| edit: false
n_layers = 3           # int    — whole numbers
conductivity = 12.4    # float  — real numbers
well_id = "A-14"       # str    — text
is_confined = True     # bool   — True / False

for value in (n_layers, conductivity, well_id, is_confined):
    print(f"{str(value):>8}  ->  {type(value).__name__}")
```

::: {.fragment}
`type()` is your first debugging tool. When something behaves strangely, ask what
it *is* before you ask why.
:::

## Types decide what operations mean

The `+` operator does entirely different things depending on what it's given:

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
print(2 + 3)          # arithmetic
print("2" + "3")      # concatenation
print(True + True)    # bool is a subclass of int. Yes, really.
```

::: {.fragment}
And sometimes it refuses:

```python
"2" + 3
# TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
```
:::

::: {.fragment}
This is the most common error you will hit in the next two weeks. It is also one
of the most useful — Python is telling you your data isn't what you thought.
:::

## Your turn: fix the type error

The depth was read from a text file, so it's a string. Fix the calculation so it
produces a number.

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_typefix
depth_text = "45.7"
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_typefix
depth_text = "45.7"
depth_below_datum = ______ + 12.0
depth_below_datum
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_typefix"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

There's a builtin that converts a string to a floating point number. It's named
after the type it produces.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_typefix"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```python
depth_below_datum = float(depth_text) + 12.0
```

Gives `57.7`. Note `int("45.7")` would *fail* — `int()` won't parse a decimal
point out of a string. `int(float("45.7"))` works and gives `45`.
:::
:::

## Two kinds of division

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
#| edit: false
print(f"17 / 5   = {17 / 5}      true division, always a float")
print(f"17 // 5  = {17 // 5}        floor division, rounds toward -inf")
print(f"17 % 5   = {17 % 5}        modulo, the remainder")
print(f"-17 // 5 = {-17 // 5}       floor, not truncation: -3 would be wrong")
```

::: {.fragment}
`//` matters when you convert coordinates to grid indices — which you will do
constantly from Week 10 onward.
:::

## Floats are approximations

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
#| edit: false
print(0.1 + 0.2)
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)
print(abs((0.1 + 0.2) - 0.3) < 1e-9)
```

::: {.fragment}
Not a bug. `0.1` has no exact binary representation, exactly as $\tfrac{1}{3}$
has no exact decimal one.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Never test floats with `==`.** Test whether the difference is small enough:

$$|a - b| < \epsilon$$

This is precisely how you'll decide an iterative solver has converged in Week 4.
:::

# Strings {background-color="#0C234B"}

## Quotes and f-strings

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
site = "USGS-09484000"
head = 412.4567

# f-strings: the f prefix lets {} interpolate expressions
print(f"Site {site} head is {head} m")
print(f"Site {site} head is {head:.2f} m")     # 2 decimal places
print(f"Site {site} head is {head:>12.2f} m")  # right-aligned, width 12
```

::: {.fragment}
Format specs matter more than they look: `:.2f` on a table of results is the
difference between a figure caption and a wall of digits.
:::

## Useful string methods

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
raw = "  A-14, Santa Cruz Basin , confined  "

print(repr(raw.strip()))
print(raw.strip().split(","))
print([part.strip() for part in raw.strip().split(",")])
print("A-14".lower(), "a-14".upper())
print("A-14_deep".replace("_", "-"))
```

::: {.fragment}
Messy real data is mostly whitespace and inconsistent case. `.strip()`,
`.split()`, and `.lower()` will carry you a long way in Week 6.
:::

# Sequences {background-color="#AB0520"}

## Lists

An ordered, changeable collection. Square brackets.

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
#| edit: false
water_levels = [412.5, 411.8, 410.9, 409.4, 408.2]

print(f"length:  {len(water_levels)}")
print(f"first:   {water_levels[0]}")
print(f"last:    {water_levels[-1]}")
print(f"minimum: {min(water_levels)}")
```

::: {.fragment}
**Indexing starts at zero.** `[0]` is the first element. `[-1]` is the last,
which is genuinely useful — no `len(x) - 1` arithmetic.
:::

## Slicing

`sequence[start:stop]` — includes `start`, **excludes** `stop`.

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
#| edit: false
water_levels = [412.5, 411.8, 410.9, 409.4, 408.2]

print(water_levels[0:3])   # first three
print(water_levels[:3])    # same thing
print(water_levels[2:])    # from index 2 to the end
print(water_levels[-2:])   # last two
```

::: {.fragment}
Half-open intervals feel wrong for about a week, then feel right forever:
`a[:n]` and `a[n:]` split a sequence with no overlap and no gap, and
`stop - start` is always the length.
:::

## Your turn: slice a timeseries

`monthly_head` holds one head measurement per month for a year, January first.
Pull out the **summer monsoon months** — July, August, September.

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_slice
monthly_head = [
    415.2, 414.8, 414.1, 413.2, 412.0, 410.6,
    409.1, 411.7, 413.9, 414.6, 415.0, 415.3,
]
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_slice
monsoon = ______
monsoon
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_slice"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 1

January is index 0, so what index is July?
:::
:::

::: {.hint exercise="ex_slice"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 2

You want three elements starting at index 6. Remember the `stop` index is
excluded, so it needs to be one past the last element you want.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_slice"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```python
monsoon = monthly_head[6:9]
```

`[409.1, 411.7, 413.9]` — the recovery after the June low, which is what
monsoon recharge looks like in a hydrograph.
:::
:::

## Lists change, tuples don't

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
levels = [412.5, 411.8]
levels.append(410.9)      # lists are mutable
print(levels)

grid_shape = (3, 40, 60)  # tuples are immutable
print(grid_shape[1])
```

::: {.fragment}
```python
grid_shape[0] = 5
# TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment
```
:::

::: {.fragment}
Use a **tuple** when the collection *is* one thing — a coordinate, a grid shape,
a row. Use a **list** when it's a growing pile of things. MODFLOW grid shapes
come back as tuples, and that's not an accident.
:::

## Dictionaries

Look things up by name instead of position.

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
#| edit: false
aquifer = {
    "name": "Santa Cruz",
    "conductivity": 12.4,
    "porosity": 0.28,
    "confined": False,
}

print(aquifer["conductivity"])
print(aquifer.get("storativity", "not measured"))  # no KeyError
print(list(aquifer.keys()))
```

::: {.fragment}
`aquifer["storativity"]` would raise `KeyError`. `.get()` with a default is how
you handle data that might be missing — a Week 6 problem you'll meet a lot.
:::

## Your turn: build a lookup

Build a dictionary mapping each well ID to its hydraulic conductivity, then look
up well `"B-07"`.

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_dict
well_ids = ["A-14", "B-07", "C-22"]
conductivities = [12.4, 3.8, 41.0]
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_dict
k_by_well = ______
k_by_well["B-07"]
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_dict"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 1

You could type the dictionary out by hand — `{"A-14": 12.4, ...}` — and that is
a perfectly good answer.
:::
:::

::: {.hint exercise="ex_dict"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 2

For the slicker version: `zip()` pairs up two sequences, and `dict()` turns a
sequence of pairs into a dictionary.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_dict"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

By hand:

```python
k_by_well = {"A-14": 12.4, "B-07": 3.8, "C-22": 41.0}
```

Or built from the two lists:

```python
k_by_well = dict(zip(well_ids, conductivities))
```

Both give `3.8`. The second scales to 3000 wells; the first doesn't. We come
back to `zip()` next week.
:::
:::

## Choosing a container {.smaller}

| You have | Use | Why |
|---|---|---|
| An ordered pile that grows | `list` | append, sort, slice |
| One fixed thing with parts | `tuple` | can't be modified by accident |
| Values you look up by name | `dict` | no index bookkeeping |
| Numbers you'll do math on | `numpy` array | **Week 4** — element-wise math |

::: {.fragment}
Lists are the wrong tool for arithmetic: `[1, 2] * 2` gives `[1, 2, 1, 2]`, not
`[2, 4]`. That's what numpy is for, and it's where we go next week.
:::
